# 2. PubTator3 Search (Entity highlighting, fallback)

for page in range(1, 10 + 1):
    search_results = pubtator_api_search_papers(
        boolean_query_text='feline parvovirus India molecular characterization genetic analysis cats FPV canine parvovirus variants',
        relation_query=None,
        page=page,
        max_retries=3,
        max_requests_per_second=3
    )
    if search_results is not None and not search_results.empty:
        pubtator_results.append(search_results)
    else:
        break

if pubtator_results:
    pubtator_df = pd.concat(pubtator_results)
    if "Highlighted_Text" in pubtator_df.columns:
        pubtator_df = pubtator_df.rename(columns={"Highlighted_Text": "Abstract"})
    
    for col in ["PMID", "Title", "Journal", "Year", "Abstract"]:
        if col not in pubtator_df.columns:
            pubtator_df[col] = ""

    df_list.append(pubtator_df)

# 3. Combine, Deduplicate and Format Clean Output

    # Deduplicate by PMID, keeping the first occurrence (which guarantees PubMed relevance is maintained)
    final_df = final_df.drop_duplicates(subset=["PMID"], keep="first")
    
    # Optional: Save to CSV for persistent logging

    print(f"The search results are saved at '/home/data4/xiangyu/BioDSA/workdir/workdir/Indian_feline_parvovirus_genetics.csv'")
    print(f"Total results found: {len(final_df)}\n")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("TOP RESULTS (Showing up to 15 most relevant):")

    # FORMAT FOR LLM: Clean text layout rather than Markdown table
    for idx, row in final_df.head(15).iterrows():
        pmid = row.get('PMID', 'N/A')
        title = row.get('Title', 'No Title')
        journal = row.get('Journal', 'Unknown')
        year = row.get('Year', 'Unknown')
        abstract = str(row.get('Abstract', 'No Abstract Available'))
        
        # Clean abstract spaces and truncate at 1200 chars to save context window
        abstract = " ".join(abstract.split())
        if len(abstract) > 1200:
            abstract = abstract[:1200] + " ... [Truncated]"
            
        print(f"PMID: {pmid}")

else:

Title: Molecular characterisation of parvoviruses from domestic cats reveals emergence of newer variants in India.

Journal/Date: Journal of feline medicine and surgery (2017)

--- ABSTRACT ---
Objectives The present study was undertaken to characterise the viral polypeptide 2 (VP2) gene of parvovirus from domestic cats in India. Methods The faecal samples from diarrhoeic/healthy domestic cats were collected from different geographical regions of India for screening by PCR assay followed by sequence analysis of the VP2 gene. Results Canine parvovirus (CPV)/feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) infections were found in 12 (11.3%) of 106 faecal samples tested. Two new CPV-2a (297Ala and Asn426) and three FPV strains were identified by VP2 gene analysis. Several unique and existing amino acid mutations were found, suggesting continuous evolution and emergence of newer variants. The phylogenetic analysis of the CPV sequences revealed that the two new CPV-2a strains from Mumbai (MC8) and Puducherry (P15) were clustered together in a single clade but had evolved independently and were ancestrally related to Chinese CPV-2a isolates. The FPV sequences (T-C-6 and T-C-1) from Thrissur, Kerala, formed a different clade (FPV clade) and were closely related to each other and had an ancestral relationship with an FPV isolate from the USA. Another FPV isolate from Goa (GC1) was positioned in the same clade but had evolved independently. Conclusions and relevance Detection of CPV in both diarrhoeic/healthy cats and the occurrence of FPV infection in a vaccinated cat provide new insights into parvovirus infections in cats in India.

Title: Molecular Epidemiology and Genetic Characterization of Feline Panleukopenia Virus among Clinically Suspected Domestic Cats in Tamil Nadu, India.

Journal/Date: Microorganisms (2026)

--- ABSTRACT ---
Feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) causes feline panleukopenia (FP), a highly contagious and often fatal disease in domestic cats. This study investigated FPV detection, associated epidemiological factors, and partial VP2 genetic characteristics among clinically suspected cats presented in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India. Exploratory molecular docking was also performed to compare predicted VP2-transferrin receptor type-1 interactions in feline and canine systems. FPV DNA was detected in 83 of 180 clinically suspected cats (46.11%). Multivariable analysis revealed higher odds of FPV PCR positivity in female cats than in male cats (aOR: 2.65; 95% CI: 1.35-5.21) and lower odds in vaccinated cats than in unvaccinated cats (aOR: 0.41; 95% CI: 0.17-0.97). Compared with summer, higher odds were observed during the southwest monsoon (aOR: 3.59; 95% CI: 1.26-10.20) and northeast monsoon (aOR: 17.11; 95% CI: 3.86-75.80), whereas age group and breed were not significantly associated with PCR positivity. FPV was successfully isolated from four of the ten PCR-positive clinical samples inoculated onto CRFK cells. Partial VP2 sequencing of 13 PCR-positive samples showed 98.1-98.5% nucleotide identity with the vaccine reference strain and identified several nucleotide and amino acid substitutions. Most study sequences clustered with Indian FPV reference strains, whereas one sequence clustered separately within the carnivore parvovirus grouping. Molecular docking of the (TfR1-VP2 interaction identified differences in the predicted interaction patterns between feline and canine complexes, with the feline complex exhibiting a more favourable ZRANK score. However, these findings represent computational predictions and require experimental validation. Overall, the study highlights the circulation of genetically diverse FPV strains in southern India and underscores the importance of continued surveillance and molecular characterization to support disease monitoring and control strategies.

key_findings.finding: The primary Indian domestic-cat study (PMID 27502089; Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery, 2017) tested feces from 106 diarrhoeic/healthy cats collected across multiple Indian regions; 12 (11.3%) were CPV/FPV-positive by PCR. VP2 analysis identified two CPV-2a strains (Mumbai MC8 and Puducherry P15, described as new and carrying 297Ala and Asn426) plus three FPV strains. CPV sequences clustered together but were independently evolved and ancestrally related to Chinese CPV-2a; FPV sequences from Kerala and Goa formed/occupied an FPV clade. Authors concluded that unique/existing amino-acid mutations indicated continuous evolution and emergence of newer variants, and highlighted CPV infection in healthy cats and FPV infection in a vaccinated cat.

The southern-India phylodynamic study (PMID 35493752; VirusDisease, 2022) characterized full-length VP2 from domestic cats and rescue-shelter cats. It found both FPV and CPV infections; five sequences had FPV-characteristic amino-acid variation and one was classified as a New CPV-2a/FPV sequence. Three previously unreported mutations were reported at VP2 amino-acid positions 303, 441, and 554, and one cat sequence showed a potential New CPV-2a/FPV recombinant signal. The authors concluded that cats can harbor CPV variants and FPV, with co-/superinfection potentially facilitating transmission, recombination, and genetic heterogeneity. This is direct evidence of recently described/emerging molecular features rather than simple identification of established variants, although the abstract does not provide sample counts or exact collection sites beyond southern India.

A Tamil Nadu study (PMID 42654988; Microorganisms, 2026) examined 180 clinically suspected domestic cats in Chennai: 83 (46.11%) were FPV-PCR-positive, four of ten inoculated PCR-positive samples were isolated in CRFK cells, and 13 positives were partially VP2-sequenced. Sequences had 98.1–98.5% nucleotide identity to the vaccine reference strain; several nucleotide/amino-acid substitutions were found, most sequences clustered with Indian FPV references, and one clustered separately within the carnivore-parvovirus grouping. The abstract supports circulation of genetically diverse FPV, but does not establish a named novel variant; therefore this study is better classified as characterization of circulating/known FPV with divergence, not a clearly demonstrated newly emerging variant. Its reported epidemiologic associations included higher positivity in females and during monsoon seasons and lower positivity in vaccinated cats.

Across the located primary literature, the evidence is mixed: the 2017 and especially 2022 studies explicitly report newer/emerging features (new CPV-2a descriptions, novel VP2 substitutions, and a potential CPV-2a/FPV recombinant), whereas the 2026 Tamil Nadu study mainly documents prevalent FPV strains related to Indian/vaccine references with substitutions and one divergent sequence, without naming a new variant. The search also located no additional clearly relevant Indian domestic-cat molecular primary study in the returned results; India-focused dog-only CPV studies and non-Indian cat studies should not be treated as direct evidence for this question.
